summary: This memo gives criteria for designing a border router that runs BGP with routers outside its network and OSPF inside it, so routes pass correctly between the two. It is historic.

eli5.summary: A gate between two towns has to translate directions from one town's map style to the other's. This paper explains how a router should do that. It is historic.

questions: how do bgp and ospf interact
how do bgp and ospf exchange routes

subtitle: Rules for a border router that speaks BGP to the outside world and OSPF inside its own network.

tldr.problem: A router on the edge of an autonomous system has to pass routes between BGP, used with neighbouring autonomous systems, and OSPF, used inside the network. The two protocols carry different information, so the translation has to be defined.
tldr.mechanism: The memo sets rules for which routes cross over (by default none), and for how OSPF cost and type, the OSPF tag, and the OSPF forwarding address map to the BGP INTER-AS METRIC, ORIGIN and AS_PATH, and NEXT_HOP attributes. It also requires the BGP identifier to equal the OSPF router ID.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1403 is a republication of RFC 1364 that fixes editorial problems, and it is now Historic.

facts.label: Default OSPF cost and type for imports

today: RFC 1403 is Historic. It republished RFC 1364 to correct editorial problems, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 1403 defines the criteria for designing an Autonomous System Border Router (ASBR) that runs BGP with ASBRs outside its autonomous system (AS) and OSPF as its interior protocol. It says how three pairs of values are set when the router sits between the two protocols: OSPF cost and type versus the BGP INTER-AS METRIC, the OSPF tag versus the BGP ORIGIN and AS_PATH, and the OSPF forwarding address versus the BGP NEXT_HOP.

The memo uses two terms carefully. An Autonomous System looks monolithic from the outside, with one coherent interior routing plan. A Routing Domain is a collection of routers that coordinate using a single instance of a routing protocol. The words MUST, SHOULD and MAY follow the Host Requirements RFCs.
sections.eli5: The router at the edge of a network has to talk to neighbours in one language and to its own network in another. This paper is the phrasebook for the border router.

sections.title: Exchanging Routes Between BGP and OSPF
sections.content:
BGP carries no subnet information, so several OSPF subnet routes for one subnetted network are collapsed into a single network route when exported into BGP. The ASBR MUST advertise that network route as long as at least one subnet is reachable via OSPF.

For exporting OSPF routes into BGP, the administrator MUST be able to filter selectively, down to a single network and by the OSPF tag and its sub-fields. The default MUST be to export nothing, and OSPF external routes of type 1 and type 2 MUST never be exported unless explicitly configured. The INTER-AS METRIC can be set statically but MUST NOT be set by default, since it is an optional attribute. If a route becomes unreachable, the ASBR MUST tell its external BGP neighbours immediately. A minimum delay between learning a route in OSPF and advertising it in BGP MUST be configurable, with a default of 0.

For importing BGP routes into OSPF, implementations SHOULD allow control per network and per autonomous system, and the default MUST be to import nothing. The OSPF cost MUST default to 1 and the metric type to type 2. Routes learned via BGP from peers in the same AS MUST NOT be imported, and the ASBR MUST NOT generate a default route into OSPF unless explicitly configured to.
sections.eli5: The border router is a careful doorman. By default it lets no routes through in either direction, and the owner has to list exactly which ones may pass.

sections.title: BGP Identifier and OSPF Router ID
sections.content:
The BGP identifier MUST be the same as the OSPF router ID at all times that the router is up. The memo gives two reasons.

The first is synchronisation. Suppose RT1 and RT2 both import a route to external network X into OSPF while RT3, in the same AS, advertises X to external BGP speakers. RT3 must find out which ASBR it uses to reach X by matching the OSPF router ID of its route with the BGP identifier of one of those ASBRs, so that it can build the correct AS_PATH. The second reason is convenience: an administrator can correlate BGP and OSPF routes by the shared identifier.
sections.eli5: If a person had one name at school and a different name at home, nobody could tell they were the same person. Using one name for both makes it easy to match things up.

sections.title: The OSPF Tag and BGP Path Attributes
sections.content:
OSPF has a 32-bit external route tag whose meaning is left open by OSPF itself. This memo uses it to rebuild the BGP ORIGIN and AS_PATH attributes when routes learned inside the AS are re-exported to other autonomous systems. The high bit is the Automatic bit. When it is 1, the tag holds a Completeness bit, a two-bit PathLength, a 12-bit ArbitraryTag (default 0) and a 16-bit AutonomousSystem number (0 means the local AS). When it is 0, the remaining 31 bits are a manually configured LocalInfo value, and nothing may be inferred about the route.

Manual tags are the default for backward compatibility, and a mechanism to turn on automatic generation MUST exist. For a manual tag the mapping is ORIGIN=INCOMPLETE and AS_PATH=local_AS. For automatic tags, PathLength 00 means a path of length zero (the usual case for an IGP), 01 means one AS is known (the usual case for EGP), and 10 means a longer path. PathLength 11 is reserved, routers MUST NOT generate it, and ASBRs MUST ignore such tags.

Routes with a longer path cannot fit in the tag. If the path information is incomplete, the route MUST NOT be re-exported into BGP at another ASBR. If it is complete, the path travels between ASBRs of the same AS by BGP, and the route MUST NOT be exported from OSPF into BGP. The ASBR must wait for the BGP update from its internal neighbours before advertising it externally.
sections.eli5: Each route carries a small label with a few boxes ticked, such as whether the full trip is known and how many towns it passes through. The border router reads the boxes to write the right note for the other side.

sections.title: Forwarding Address and NEXT_HOP
sections.content:
Forwarding addresses avoid extra hops between routers that share a network but speak different protocols. BGP has the well-known mandatory NEXT_HOP attribute, and OSPF has a Forwarding Address field.

The memo's example has RT1 and RT2 in one AS and RT3 and RT4 in another, all on a common network. RT1 and RT3 speak BGP, and RT3 and RT4 speak OSPF. When RT3 imports external network X learned from RT1, it MUST always copy the BGP NEXT_HOP into the OSPF Forwarding Address. When RT3 exports a network Y that is internal to its OSPF domain and reached via RT4, it MUST set NEXT_HOP to RT4's address (if Y is not a subnetted network), so packets do not take an extra hop through RT3.
sections.eli5: If the shortcut to a house is through the neighbour's gate, the border router tells visitors to go straight to that gate instead of walking through its own first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo's security section is one sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. It sets no authentication or protection requirements for the exchange of routes between the two protocols.
sections.eli5: The paper says nothing about locks or guards. It only explains the translation rules.

viz.caption: OSPF TAG WITH THE AUTOMATIC BIT SET (RFC 1403)

fields.name: a
fields.desc: Automatic bit: Completeness and PathLength were generated by a router.

fields.name: c
fields.desc: Completeness: the source of the incoming route is known precisely.

fields.name: pl
fields.desc: PathLength: zero, one or more than one AS in the path; 11 is reserved.

fields.name: ArbitraryTag
fields.desc: Defaults to 0 but can be configured.

fields.name: AutonomousSystem
fields.desc: AS number for the route; 0 for the local AS.
